content.description: From March 18 to May 28, 1871, Paris governed itself for **72 days**. The experiment ended in the Bloody Week, a crackdown that left a lasting mark on French memory.

hero.hook: 72 days when Paris ruled itself, before being crushed in blood.

blocks.text: From **March 18** to **May 28, 1871**, Paris lived through a rare experiment: the **Commune**. For **72 days**, the capital governed itself. It refused to obey the government based in **Versailles** and tried out a more social kind of democracy.
The uprising was born from a national defeat, a starving siege and a split between a radical Paris and a more conservative countryside. It ended with the **Bloody Week**.

It all started with the [[Franco-Prussian War]] (**1870-1871**). The French emperor **Napoleon III** was captured at **Sedan**. Paris then endured a four-month siege. People ate horses, zoo animals, then rats. The surrender felt humiliating.

blocks.caption: Paris barricades during the Commune of 1871

blocks.text: At Christmas **1870**, some luxury restaurants served elephant consomme or kangaroo stew, taken from the menagerie of the city's botanical garden.

In February, [[Adolphe Thiers]] led an assembly that was mostly monarchist and had withdrawn to Versailles. On **March 18**, he tried to seize the cannons of the [[National Guard]], a militia of armed Parisians, stored at **Montmartre**. The crowd fraternized with the soldiers. Thiers pulled his troops out of Paris. A Central Committee took control of the city.

sections.title: After the defeat and the siege

blocks.text: On **March 28**, the Commune was proclaimed. Workers, craftsmen, journalists and men close to the [[International Workingmen's Association]], a network of unions and workers' parties, made laws at speed. Rent debts were canceled. Night work for bakers was abolished. Abandoned workshops were handed to cooperatives.

blocks.caption: The Hôtel de Ville, political heart of the Commune

blocks.text: It also proclaimed the separation of church and state and free, secular schooling, and it had the **Vendôme Column** pulled down as a symbol of the Empire. [[Louise Michel]], a teacher and activist, embodied the central role of women in the political clubs and on the barricades.

On **May 21**, the Versailles troops entered Paris. This was the **Bloody Week**. District by district, barricade after barricade, the repression was ferocious. Hostages were shot. The Tuileries and the Hôtel de Ville burned.

blocks.caption: The Bloody Week: Paris retaken street by street

blocks.text: During the Commune, the red flag became the official emblem of Paris, replacing the tricolor, judged too close to the governments that had surrendered.

The [[Fédérés]], the name given to the supporters of the Commune, fell back to the **Père-Lachaise** cemetery. There, **147** last fighters were shot against the **Communards' Wall**. The toll: between **10,000 and 30,000** dead in one week, followed by deportations to New Caledonia.

For the philosopher **Karl Marx** and the International, the Commune was the first experiment in workers' power. Its defeat, though, strengthened a **Third Republic** built on “order.” Some Communard ideas, such as secularism and social rights, returned later in republican law.

blocks.text: In **72 days**, the Paris Commune tried out a radical social democracy, before being wiped out in the Bloody Week, at the cost of tens of thousands of lives.

1870-1871.explanation: Conflict triggered by Napoleon III, ending with the crushing defeat at Sedan and the capture of the Emperor. The humiliating capitulation and the siege of Paris created the breeding ground for the Commune.

Adolphe Thiers.explanation: Head of the provisional government in Versailles who ordered the crushing of the Commune during the "Bloody Week" (May 21-28, 1871). A former journalist and historian, he was the first president of the Third Republic.

First International.explanation: Organization founded in London in 1864, bringing together trade unions and workers' parties from several countries. Although the Commune was not its direct work, Marx celebrated it as the first experience of workers' power.

Franco-Prussian War.explanation: Conflict triggered by Napoleon III, ending with the crushing defeat at Sedan and the capture of the Emperor. The humiliating capitulation and the siege of Paris created the breeding ground for the Commune.

Franco-Prussian War (1870-1871).explanation: Conflict triggered by Napoleon III, ending with the crushing defeat at Sedan and the capture of the Emperor. The humiliating capitulation and the siege of Paris created the breeding ground for the Commune.

Fédérés.explanation: Name given to the supporters of the Paris Commune, as they claimed to belong to a federation of autonomous communes.

International Workingmen's Association.explanation: Organization founded in London in 1864, bringing together trade unions and workers' parties from several countries. Although the Commune was not its direct work, Marx celebrated it as the first experience of workers' power.

Louise Michel.explanation: Nicknamed the 'Red Virgin', she is one of the major figures of the Commune, an anarchist activist and ambulance driver on the barricades.

National Guard.explanation: Citizen militia composed mainly of Parisians, with its own weapons and elected leaders. In 1871, it becomes the armed wing of the Commune.
